title: Would A Love Drug Be Ethical?
summary: Josh and Chuck (with the transcript's iHeart Intro speaker, who appears to be Josh or Chuck) discuss "love drugs": hypothetical pharmaceuticals that could strengthen or weaken romantic love in long-term partnerships. They cover Helen Fisher's three-part model of love (lust, romantic attraction, attachment) and the brain chemicals tied to each (testosterone/estrogen, dopamine, norepinephrine, cortisol, serotonin, oxytocin, vasopressin). They discuss Lisa Diamond's split attraction model, philosophers Julian Savulescu and Brian Earp and their book "Love Drugs," existing substances (alcohol, Viagra, SSRIs, intranasal oxytocin, MDMA in therapy), prairie vole research, and ethical objections from Sven Nyholm, Jacob Blair, Heikki Nara, and Peter Harrison Kelly, plus misuse concerns such as conversion therapy. The episode ends with listener mail correcting the singer and writer of "Santa's Got a Brand New Bag."
topics: Helen Fisher three stages of love

entities.name: Love Drugs: The Chemical Future of Relationships

segments.title: Opening and setup for love drugs
segments.summary: The hosts introduce love drugs, the philosophers Savulescu and Earp and their book, and the premise that love has a biochemical basis that could be manipulated.

segments.title: Helen Fisher's three stages of love and Lisa Diamond's split model
segments.summary: Fisher divides romantic love into lust, romantic attraction, and attachment. Lisa Diamond argues sex and romantic attraction are functionally independent, challenging Fisher's single-package view.
topics: Helen Fisher three stages of love

segments.title: Brain chemicals behind attraction and attachment
segments.summary: Testosterone and estrogen drive libido; dopamine, norepinephrine, cortisol and serotonin drive romantic attraction; oxytocin and vasopressin drive attachment and bonding.

segments.title: Framing: enhancing long-term love, not creating it
segments.summary: The hosts explain that love drugs would not be love potions from fairy tales but tools for long-term couples to boost feelings they have lost.

segments.title: Why support monogamy and comparisons to vacations and dinners
segments.summary: Savulescu and Earp compare love drugs to vacations and dinners that couples already use. They argue long-term coupling benefits health, while acknowledging that some people, such as those with autism or ADHD, may struggle with attachment.

segments.title: Medical community and SSRIs affecting partners
segments.summary: The hosts note that SSRIs can dampen libido and feelings, affecting partners, and that the medical community treats patients as individuals rather than couples.

segments.title: Pharmaceuticals for enhancement versus treatment
segments.summary: The philosophers question the dichotomy that drugs are only for treating disease, and warn that a love drug market could invent a new condition such as hypolovia.

segments.title: Live show aside
segments.summary: Brief banter about a live show inside joke and the release timing of that episode.

segments.title: Existing drugs: alcohol, Viagra, prairie voles
segments.summary: Alcohol is already used socially on dates. Viagra and testosterone are libido drugs. Prairie voles bond through oxytocin and vasopressin, and lab experiments show drugs can induce bonding.

segments.title: Intranasal oxytocin, trust, and military uses
segments.summary: Intranasal oxytocin spray is already on the market and may have effects. Oxytocin early studies show replication problems. Air Force major David Dethlefs proposed oxytocin for hostage negotiation and riot control.

segments.title: MDMA in therapy
segments.summary: MDMA releases oxytocin, dopamine and other chemicals. It was banned for therapeutic study in 1985 but is still used in some settings, including couples therapy and PTSD treatment, and anecdotal reports describe lasting attachment.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode ad break with a light joke about jazz musicians.

segments.title: Anti-love drugs for ending harmful attachments
segments.summary: The philosophers propose drugs to help people leave toxic or abusive relationships, and the hosts list other uses such as breaking harmful attachments, which they see as the least objectionable use.

segments.title: Ethical objections: Nyholm, Blair, Nara
segments.summary: Sven Nyholm argues chemically produced love is not real love even with good side effects. Jacob Blair argues love does not depend on the partner's true characteristics. Heikki Nara argues side effects could still keep people together.

segments.title: Peter Harrison Kelly on attachment as a feeling
segments.summary: Bioethicist Peter Harrison Kelly argues attachment is not simply a drive and that hormones only boost the trappings of attachment, which supports the philosophers' position.

segments.title: Misuse risks and conversion therapy
segments.summary: The hosts raise misuse concerns, including spiking drinks and conversion therapy. Critics said the philosophers were naive about regulation.

segments.title: Listener mail: Santa's Got a Brand New Bag
segments.summary: A listener corrects the hosts: the song is by Bob Seger and the Last Heard, not James Brown or James Taylor, released in 1966 on Cameo Parkway. A second song with the same title by Joe Chanal circus is also mentioned.
topics: Santa's Got a Brand New Bag
